issue.title: Should a childhood conviction follow you for life?
issue.question: Should a conviction from childhood stop showing up on job and college checks, and if so, after how long?
issue.summary: On 12 November 2026 the Ministry of Justice opened a consultation on changing how childhood criminal records are disclosed in England and Wales. The proposals include ending lifelong disclosure for non-listed childhood convictions with custodial sentences of two years or less (an 11-year period instead), removing automatic disclosure of out-of-court resolutions, and cutting the period fines show up. Serious violent and sexual offences would still always be disclosed. Responses are due by 24 December 2026.

bench.title: Keep the checks; add a spent date, a review panel and a safeguard lock
bench.answer: The Ministry of Justice keeps today's disclosure checks but changes the rules inside them. Minor childhood convictions drop off standard and enhanced checks after a fixed period, as proposed (s2). Serious violent and sexual offences stay on every check (s1). Checks for child-safety and care work keep full disclosure. Anyone refused a drop-off can ask a small independent panel to look at their record. The Youth Justice Board would publish yearly how many childhood records show on checks, using the same measure the consultation uses (s2). It worked if that share falls while safeguarding referrals do not rise.

bench.title: Give childhood records to an independent panel, not Whitehall
bench.answer: Move decisions on hiding childhood records from the Ministry's fixed rules to an independent youth records panel, with a youth justice specialist, a care-sector safeguarding lead and someone with a childhood record. Government sets the floor: serious violent and sexual offences always show (s1, s2). The panel reviews each other record, as 19 simulated citizens asked, and can add explanation support for employers, as 10 asked. Checks for child-safety and care work stay at least as strict (20 backers). We'd know it worked if the share of checks disclosing a childhood offence (0.71% standard, 0.35% enhanced, s2) falls while serious offences stay disclosed.

bench.title: A clear expiry date, with applicants steering enforcement
bench.answer: End lifelong disclosure for eligible childhood convictions carrying custody of two years or less. Set the limit at 11 years from conviction, as proposed in s2. Keep serious violent and sexual offences disclosed, and preserve safeguards for child-safety and care work. Let applicants run local advice groups that help challenge expired records on job and college checks. Give these groups power to demand corrections, with checking firms paying correction costs when they get it wrong. Judge success by fewer expired records appearing, quicker corrections, and more applicants reaching work or study. Publish anonymous results each year.

jury.question: Who should decide when a childhood record stops showing on checks: a fixed rule, an independent panel, or people who use the system?
options: A fixed number of years for everyone
An independent panel looking at each record
Applicant-run groups with power to force corrections
jury.ruling: A fixed number of years for everyone: five jurors chose it because a clear date is the same for everyone and does not depend on who reviews it.

reasons.text: A set number of years is clear and the same for everyone. Judges and panels vary.
Fixed years, with serious crimes still shown. Keep it simple and cheap.
A panel can see whether someone has really changed. A date cannot.
If you did it, it stays. Employers have a right to know.

minister.trial: In the reply to the consultation, back a fixed filtering period for non-listed childhood convictions with custody of two years or less. Serious violent and sexual offences, and child-safety and care checks, stay as they are. Review after one year.
minister.fail_number: If the share of standard checks disclosing a childhood offence (0.71% now) does not fall, or any serious offence stops showing, it failed.
minister.statement:
The jury chose a fixed date over a panel or a lifetime record. Five of twelve, so not a landslide.

A date is clear and the same for everyone. The cost is that it ignores the person.

So we start small: minor convictions only. Serious violent and sexual offences stay on every check. Care and child-safety checks do not get weaker.

The size of it: under 1 in 100 standard checks shows a childhood offence. We will count again in a year.
